name: Amiga 1200
description: Commodore's last mass-market Amiga, released in October 1992. It brought the AGA chipset and a 32-bit 68EC020 to the familiar wedge-shaped home computer, with 256-colour screens and an internal IDE hard-drive port. Commodore went bankrupt in 1994, cutting its life short.

specs.graphics: AGA: 256 colours from 16.8 million, HAM8 mode up to 262,144

curiosities: The Amiga CD32 console was built on essentially the same AGA hardware.
It has a PCMCIA Type II slot on its side, used for RAM cards and network adapters.
After Commodore's 1994 bankruptcy, the German company Escom bought the Amiga rights and put the A1200 back into production.
Its HAM8 mode can show up to 262,144 colours on screen at once.
story: The Amiga began in 1982 as Hi-Toro, a small Californian company led by Jay Miner, the designer of Atari's 8-bit chips, which set out to build a games machine around custom chips. Out of money, it was bought by Commodore in 1984, and the Amiga 1000 arrived in 1985 with colour, sound and multitasking far ahead of the PC and Mac of the day.

The A1200 came in late 1992 with the AGA chipset: 256 colours on screen from a palette of 16.8 million and a 68020 processor, in the same wedge case as the hugely popular A500. In Europe, and above all in Britain, it carried a scene of bedroom coders and studios such as Team17, Psygnosis, DMA Design and the Bitmap Brothers.

Commodore went bankrupt in April 1994, and the Amiga never had a true successor. Its games, its demoscene and its tracker music outlived it, and studios that started on it went on to make Lemmings, Worms and Grand Theft Auto.
